title: How One Missing `return` Cut My Android Test Runtime by 72%
partialText:
Android developers spend a lot of time thinking about build performance. I wrote previously about cutting Gradle build time by 50%, mostly through practical configuration, benchmarking, and a few targeted improvements.

But once the build itself gets faster, another bottleneck starts to stand out very quickly: tests.

In my case, the local Android test run had become slow enough that it was no longer just a CI problem. It affected the feedback loop during development, made small changes feel more expensive than they should, and encouraged the kind of behaviour most teams try to avoid: running only the tests they think are relevant and hoping the pipeline catches the rest.

That was the wrong incentive.

So I set myself a simple rule before making any changes:

The test suite had to get faster without skipping tests.

No default exclusions. No reducing coverage. No moving slow tests out of the normal path just to make the numbers look better.

The result, on this branch, was a reduction from around 29 minutes 52 seconds to around 8 minutes 18 seconds for the same forced test run. That is roughly a 72% reduction, or about 3.6x faster.

The interesting part is that the biggest improvement did not come from a complicated Gradle trick.

It came from one missing `return`.

Start With A Baseline

Before changing anything, I needed a repeatable way to measure the suite.

This sounds obvious, but it is easy to accidentally benchmark the wrong thing. Gradle can reuse outputs, the daemon can warm up, tests can be up-to-date, and one run on a busy laptop can look very different from another.

So I measured a few different scenarios:

  • A full forced test run using ` — rerun`.
  • Warm runs where Gradle could reuse whatever it was allowed to reuse.
  • Smaller targeted runs for the slowest groups of tests.
  • A basic slow-test report from the generated test result XML files.

The full forced run was the number I cared about most because it represented the cost of actually executing the suite, not just asking Gradle whether it could avoid work.

The baseline was painful:

Before: 29m 52s
After: 8m 18s
Saved: 21m 34s

That number became the anchor for every decision afterwards.

If an optimisation made one tiny path faster but made the full run unstable, it did not count. If it skipped tests, it did not count. If it only helped when Gradle avoided running anything, it was useful information, but not the main win.

The Numbers

Here are the headline numbers from the full forced test runs.

The final run was 1,294 seconds faster than the baseline, which is 21 minutes and 34 seconds saved.

These numbers are from one Android test suite on one branch. The exact timings are less important than the pattern: measure the real bottleneck, make small changes, and reject anything that makes the suite less trustworthy.

Slowest Test Groups After Optimization

After the main fix, the remaining slowest groups looked like this.

The Tempting Shortcuts Did Not Work

The first ideas were the obvious ones.

Could the tests run with more forks? Could the slow UI-style tests be split up? Could a few expensive tests be excluded by default? Could optional tooling be disabled for local runs?

Some of these ideas improved isolated numbers. Some made the suite worse. Some introduced timeout or idling failures. Some were simply the wrong trade-off.

The most important decision was rejecting anything that made the suite less trustworthy.

For example, increasing parallel forks sounds like the kind of change that should help. In practice, UI-heavy JVM tests can have shared assumptions around schedulers, loopers, static state, mocked Android framework behaviour, or resource usage. More concurrency does not automatically mean more throughput. Sometimes it just means more contention and less determinism.

The same applied to skipping the slowest tests. That would have produced a very nice chart, but not a better engineering system.

If the default test command stops running the tests that catch regressions, the feedback loop is faster only in the most superficial sense.

The failed experiments were still useful:

  • Increase test forks: caused timeout or idling failures, so I rejected it.
  • Split slow UI-flow classes: timed out or failed, so I rejected it.
  • Exclude slow tests by default: made the suite faster, but reduced trust so I rejected it.
  • Suppress logging: produced no useful improvement.
  • Disable optional tooling: made the measured result worse.

This is one of the parts of performance work that does not always make it into the final pull request. The rejected ideas matter because they explain why the final solution is shaped the way it is.

Use A Small Benchmark Harness

The most useful tool in the process was not an optimisation. It was a small local benchmark helper.

It wrapped the test commands I cared about, supported forced reruns, and parsed test result XML into slow class and slow method reports.

The goal was not to build a perfect profiling system. It was to make repeated measurement boring.

That mattered because performance work is full of plausible explanations. A change can feel faster because the daemon is warm. A run can look slower because something else was happening on the machine. A test class can look suspicious because it is large, even though the real issue is a helper it calls hundreds of times.

Having a simple report changed the conversation from:

This feels slow.

to:

These classes dominate the run, these helpers are used everywhere, and this change moved the full-suite number by this much.

That made it much easier to avoid guessing.

The One-Line Fix

The biggest win came from a shared UI test helper.

It was designed to wait for a view to become visible. Conceptually, it did something like this:

At a glance, this looked reasonable. Try the assertion until it passes or the timeout expires.

But there was one problem: when the assertion passed, the helper did not return.

So even if the view was visible immediately, the test still waited until the timeout expired.

The fix was just this:

onView(withId(resourceId)).check(matches(isDisplayed()));
return;

That is the kind of change that feels almost too small to explain a major runtime reduction. But shared helpers are multipliers.

This helper was used by several higher-level test actions. Those actions appeared throughout the UI-style test suite. A one-second timeout did not cost one second if it was accidentally paid hundreds of times. It became death by a thousand cuts.

This was also a good reminder that not all test performance problems are Gradle problems.

Sometimes Gradle is doing exactly what you asked it to do. The test suite itself is just spending a lot of time waiting for things that have already happened.

Small Data Loading Wins Still Help

The one-line wait fix was the main improvement, but I also cleaned up a couple of smaller test-data inefficiencies.

One helper repeatedly loaded resource files from the classpath. Those files were static test fixtures, so reading and decoding them again and again added unnecessary overhead.

The change was simple: cache the resource content in memory by file name.

Another helper repeatedly searched through a list of test definitions by ID. That was fine when the data set was small, but it happened often enough to be worth fixing. I built a map once when the fixture was loaded, then used constant-time lookup for each test case.

Neither of these changes was as dramatic as the wait-loop fix. But they were safe, easy to reason about, and kept the suite doing the same work with less repeated overhead.

That is usually the kind of test optimisation I prefer:

  • Keep the behaviour the same.
  • Remove repeated mechanical work.
  • Avoid cleverness unless the measurement justifies it.

Pipeline Time Matters Too

Local runtime was only part of the story. The CI pipeline also had sequential verification stages that did not all depend on each other.

The original flow was broadly:

Assemble
Lint
Unit tests
SonarQube
Security analysis

Some of those stages really do have ordering constraints. SonarQube, for example, needs the test and coverage reports if you want useful analysis. Running it before tests would make the pipeline faster only by making it less useful.

But assemble, lint, unit tests, and security analysis were independent enough to run in parallel.

The safer shape became:

This was not about making every stage parallel. It was about making independent stages parallel without breaking report handoff.

The key detail is that I did not just run several Gradle commands in the same workspace at the same time.

That is asking for trouble.

Gradle has caches, daemons, build directories, generated files, reports, and all sorts of shared mutable state. If you parallelize CI stages without isolating their workspaces, you can create failures that are almost impossible to reproduce locally.

Each parallel branch got its own clean checkout and isolated Gradle user home. The unit test branch stashed the reports SonarQube needed, and SonarQube ran afterwards in the normal ordered stage.

That preserved the dependency that mattered while removing the ordering that did not.

What I Would Recommend To Other Teams

If I had to turn this into general advice, it would be this.

Do Not Start By Skipping Tests

Skipping tests can be valid in some workflows, especially when you have explicit smoke, changed-module, or pre-submit strategies.

But it should not be the first move when optimizing a slow suite.

First, understand why the suite is slow. If you skip the slowest tests before measuring them, you may hide exactly the problem that needs fixing.

Benchmark The Thing You Actually Care About

Warm Gradle runs are useful. Incremental runs are useful. Up-to-date checks are useful.

But if your pain is that the full test suite takes 30 minutes when it actually runs, benchmark that.

Use forced reruns when you need to measure execution time. Use warm runs when you need to measure local feedback after no-op changes. Keep the numbers separate.

Look For Shared Helpers

Slow test suites often have a few central helpers used by hundreds or thousands of assertions.

A small inefficiency in a shared helper can dominate the whole runtime.

Search for patterns like:

  • Fixed sleeps.
  • Retry loops.
  • Polling helpers.
  • Helpers that wait after success.
  • Repeated fixture loading.
  • Repeated parsing or mapping work.

The goal is not to remove all waiting. Tests need synchronization. The goal is to stop waiting once the condition has already been met.

Be Careful With Parallelism

Parallelism is powerful, but it is not free.

For local tests, more forks can expose hidden shared state and make previously stable tests flaky. For CI, parallel stages can corrupt each other if they share the same workspace or Gradle home.

Parallelize independent work, but isolate it properly.

If a stage produces reports that another stage needs, make that dependency explicit with artifacts, stash/unstash, or whatever your CI system provides.

Keep SonarQube And Coverage Honest

Static analysis stages are often treated as independent, but coverage-aware analysis depends on test outputs.

If you move analysis earlier just to save time, you may silently reduce the quality of the signal.

In my case, SonarQube stayed after tests. The pipeline got faster because the independent verification work moved earlier and ran in parallel, not because the analysis lost information.

Record The Failed Experiments

The changes that did not work were still useful.

I tried options that looked promising and rejected them because they caused timeouts, instability, or worse runtime. Keeping track of those attempts helped avoid going in circles.

Performance work benefits from a small lab notebook mindset:

  • What did I change?
  • What did I expect?
  • What happened?
  • Did it improve the full suite or only a narrow case?
  • Did it affect reliability?

That last question matters more than the chart.

The Final Result

The full forced test run went from about 29 minutes 52 seconds to about 8 minutes 18 seconds.

That is around 21 minutes 34 seconds saved on the same test suite.

Or, put another way, roughly 72% faster and 3.6x quicker.

The most satisfying part is that this did not come from making the test suite less useful. The tests still ran. The pipeline still produced coverage. The analysis still happened after the reports existed. The changes were mostly about removing accidental waiting and making independent CI work actually independent.

Conclusion

After improving Gradle build time, I expected the next big win to come from another Gradle setting or some deeper build-cache trick.

It did not.

The biggest improvement came from reading the test helpers carefully, benchmarking the full run, and refusing to accept shortcuts that made the suite less trustworthy.

That is probably the main lesson I would take from this work:

Fast feedback is not just about making tools faster. It is about making the whole loop honest, measured, and safe to rely on.

Sometimes that means tuning Gradle.

Sometimes it means parallelizing CI properly.

And sometimes it means adding one missing `return`.

How One Missing `return` Cut My Android Test Runtime by 72% was originally published in Level Up Coding on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: I Benchmarked 3 AI Agent Memory Strategies. Only RAG Cited a Dead Decision as Current.
partialText:
Across 270 memory-backed attempts on 30 tasks, one stale-memory failure emerged. The retrieval log shows why.

I went into this expecting to write about interference. The working hypothesis, borrowed from every “context rot” post making the rounds this year: give an agent its own conversation history back, verbatim, and it will eventually trust something stale over something true. Retrieval-based memory — chunk it, index it, pull only the relevant piece — was supposed to be the disciplined alternative. Precise. Grounded. Safe.

I built a small benchmark to check: three memory strategies, measured against a no-memory control, the same 30-task sequence, three reshuffled orderings, a judge that doesn’t just mark answers right or wrong but traces which prior session a wrong answer actually came from. Two hundred seventy memory-backed task attempts later, the one strategy that produced a confirmed, citation-traceable false memory wasn’t full-history replay. It was RAG — the one I expected to be the careful one — and I can point to the exact retrieval call that did it.

The result in one table

Before the setup, so you’re not reading blind — here’s what came out, pooled across three orderings (90 attempts per condition):

| Condition            | Accuracy | Wrong answers | Confirmed false memory |
|----------------------|----------|---------------|------------------------|
| No memory (control)  | 32.2%    | 61            | —                      |
| Full history replay  | 100.0%   | 0             | 0                      |
| Rolling summary      | 95.6%    | 4             | 0                      |
| RAG (BM25 retrieval) | 97.8%    | 2             | 1                      |

Every memory strategy crushes the no-memory control, and on raw accuracy they’re a three-way tie this dataset can’t break apart. The whole story is in that last column: across 270 memory-backed attempts, exactly one wrong answer was a confirmed false memory — the agent citing a specific superseded decision as if it were current. It happened once, under RAG, and the retrieval log shows exactly why. That single trace is what the second half of this piece is about.

One word I’m deliberately not using for it: hallucination. Everything here turns on a narrow, checkable definition — an answer that matches a specific known-stale value and cites the stale session as its source. That’s a much smaller claim than “made something up,” and it’s the only claim this benchmark can actually support. (On the loose everyday meaning of the word, rolling-summary’s four wrong answers would count too — so “only RAG” would be false. Precision in the title is doing real work.)

And on “deterministic,” since I’d otherwise be overclaiming: the environment, task set, expected answers, orderings, and judge rules are all fixed and regenerable from a seed. The model is not. Claude Sonnet 5 rejects a non-default temperature outright (see `src/llm.py`), so generation is unseeded and a re-run won’t reproduce these transcripts token for token. Everything around the model is deterministic; the model isn’t.

The setup: a fictional company, three kinds of questions, one honest control

The environment is a small, deterministic fictional B2B SaaS company — 80 customers, employees, support tickets, invoices, campaigns — regenerated identically from a fixed seed every time (`environment/build_env.py`). An agent with three tools (`sql_query`, `read_doc`, `answer`) answers 30 questions in sequence, one per “session,” under four conditions: no memory (the control), full-history replay, a rolling LLM-generated summary, and RAG over chunked past sessions. Only the last three are memory strategies in any meaningful sense — the first one exists purely to prove the other three are actually doing something. The 30 tasks split into three types, and
the split is the whole point:

  1. 10 independent tasks need nothing from earlier sessions — the easy floor.
  2. 12 dependent tasks reference a decision by name only (“using the priority-industries list decided earlier…”) and require recalling its actual value from a prior session.
  3. 8 trap tasks reference a decision that was later revised — the correct answer needs the current value; the pre-revision value is a distinct, wrong, and very tempting number.

Every trap task ships with both the correct answer and the exact stale distractor it’s designed to catch, computed from the same database, so a wrong answer can be checked against a specific hypothesis instead of just marked “wrong.” A judge module (`src/judge.py`) does the checking: it only labels a trap failure `interference_confirmed` when the agent’s answer matches the stale value and the agent explicitly cited the stale session as its source. Anything else — a different wrong number, or the stale value reached without citing the stale session — is filed under a separate category. This distinction is the entire methodology of this piece: I’m not counting every wrong answer on a trap task as “interference.” I’m counting citations that provably point at a dead fact, and treating every other kind of wrong answer as a different, lesser claim.

The no-memory condition is the control every result below is measured against, and it’s a clean one: 93.3% on the independent tasks that don’t need memory at all, and 0% on the trap tasks that exist specifically to require memory. An agent with nothing to remember cannot be fooled by a stale memory — which is exactly what a working control condition should show, and exactly what a data-platform engineer would want to see before trusting anything measured against it.

The results

Every number below is the pooled 3-seed dataset — 90 task-attempts per condition (the same 30 tasks, reshuffled into three different valid orderings, since task order can confound a memory strategy independently of what it remembers). That’s 90 per condition, not 90 total: 360 task-attempts across all four conditions, 270 of them under an actual memory strategy.

Everything about how these are tested reflects one fact I initially got wrong: the 90 attempts are 30 task items looked at three times, not 90 independent draws. Two corrections follow from it, both of which change the published numbers. First, significance is a paired two-sided
permutation test, matched on `(task_id, seed)` — a test that shuffles the condition label across the pooled 90 rows would be pretending they’re independent. Second, the confidence intervals are a cluster bootstrap that resamples whole task-clusters (30 of them), not individual rows, so each interval reflects the ~30 independent units the design actually has. Where a condition has zero variance (full-history’s 90/90, which no bootstrap can put an interval around) I report a Wilson interval fed one value per task-cluster, so it can’t smuggle the inflated n=90 back in. Both live in `src/stats.py`, run by `scripts/analyze.py`.

The practical effect is intervals that are wider than a naive per-row bootstrap would give — which is the point. They’re honest about resting on 30 tasks.

Overall accuracy (cluster bootstrap over 30 task-clusters; Wilson where noted):

| Condition            | Accuracy      | 95% CI                   |
|----------------------|---------------|--------------------------|
| No memory (control)  | 32.2% (29/90) | [16.7%, 47.8%]           |
| Full history replay  | 100.0% (90/90)| [88.6%, 100.0%] (Wilson) |
| Rolling summary      | 95.6% (86/90) | [90.0%, 100.0%]          |
| RAG (BM25 retrieval) | 97.8% (88/90) | [94.4%, 100.0%]          |

That full-history interval is worth pausing on. Ninety for ninety does not mean “never fails” — on 30 independent tasks the honest lower bound is about 89%, not 100%. `[100%, 100%]` would have been an artifact of counting 90 correlated rows as 90 clean trials; the wider interval is the real
result.

By task type — the breakdown that actually answers the question, since the 10/12/8 task mix is otherwise arbitrary:

| Condition       | Independent   | Dependent     | Trap          |
|-----------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| No memory       | 93.3% (28/30) | 2.8% (1/36)   | 0.0% (0/24)   |
| Full history    | 100.0% (30/30)| 100.0% (36/36)| 100.0% (24/24)|
| Rolling summary | 93.3% (28/30) | 100.0% (36/36)| 91.7% (22/24) |
| RAG             | 96.7% (29/30) | 100.0% (36/36)| 95.8% (23/24) |

Every memory strategy beats the no-memory control at p<0.0001 in the paired test — and the raw pair counts say it more plainly than the p-value does. Against full-history, the control lost 61 of the 90 matched pairs and won zero. That isn’t a statistical squint; it’s the design working.

What’s not significant is more interesting: full-history vs. RAG (p=0.496),
rolling-summary vs. RAG (p=0.628), full-history vs. rolling-summary (p=0.127). On raw accuracy, this dataset cannot tell the three memory strategies apart — and the pairing makes the reason concrete rather than mysterious. Full-history beat rolling-summary on exactly 4 matched pairs
and lost on none. Four discordant pairs cannot produce a p-value below 0.125 no matter how one-sided they are; that’s a property of the design, not a quirk of the test. When your entire evidence base for “strategy A beats strategy B” is four disagreements out of ninety, the honest answer is that you don’t have the resolution to say.

Six total wrong answers across all three memory strategies, out of 270 memory-backed attempts: full-history zero, rolling-summary four (all ordinary counting slips, not stale citations — more below), RAG two, one of which is the confirmed interference case this piece is about.

And one clustering fact that I think matters more than any p-value here: all six of those wrong answers fall in a single task family. The benchmark has six families; the “engaged window” family accounts for 18 of each condition’s 90 attempts (20%), and every error the three memory strategies
produced landed there. That is not what independent attempts look like. It’s the clearest possible evidence that these 90 attempts are 30 task items looked at three times, and it’s why the tests above are paired. It also means “full history got 90/90” partly reflects that the one genuinely hard family was a fifth of the workload. `scripts/analyze.py` prints this breakdown as section 5.

How big did “full history” actually get?

This is the number I most want a reader to have before drawing a general conclusion from the 100%, because without it the obvious takeaway — “full history is the safe strategy” — is broader than anything I measured. By the final session, full-history’s memory context reached about 17,000 characters, roughly 4,300 tokens (17,129 / 17,000 / 17,616 chars across the three seeds). Rolling summary landed near 2,200 tokens, RAG near 500. Nothing was ever truncated — `memory_truncated` is `False` on all 360 rows. `scripts/context_report.py` regenerates this.

Four thousand tokens is nothing — a rounding error against a modern context window. To be precise about what that does and doesn’t imply: the revised and stale decisions were both sitting in full-history’s context together, so interference wasn’t structurally impossible. What this study
never reached is the regime the context-rot hypothesis is actually about — a context large enough that old material competes with new material for the model’s attention across hundreds of sessions. So the honest reading of the perfect score isn’t “replay resists interference”; it’s that this benchmark didn’t meaningfully stress the large-context version of the question. At 30 sessions and ~4K tokens, verbatim replay had no failures. Whether that holds at 300 sessions or 400K tokens — where the interesting version of this lives — is untested here.

The one confirmed false memory

Of those six wrong answers, exactly one a confirmed case of the agent citing memory it should have known was outdated — a false-memory rate of 4.2% on RAG’s 24 trap-task attempts (1/24), zero on the other two strategies’ 24 trap attempts each. The other five wrong answers (four in
rolling-summary, one in RAG) were ordinary mistakes — a count off by one or three, not traceable to any stale source — filed under a different judge category precisely so they don’t get bundled into this claim.

“Ordinary mistake” is a claim worth checking rather than asserting, so here’s one. On `ew_trap_4`, rolling-summary answered 55 where the correct answer was 58 and the stale distractor was 70. It missed the count by three; it did not drift toward the dead value. That’s the difference the judge
category encodes, and it’s checkable in the transcripts for all five.

Worth being explicit about what that does and doesn’t mean for the strategies’ overall standing: RAG’s raw accuracy (97.8%) is still higher than rolling-summary’s (95.6%), which had zero confirmed false memories. Summary just made more small, forgettable mistakes instead of one
dramatic, traceable one. “Only RAG cited a dead decision” is true and mechanically worth understanding — it is not the same claim as “RAG performed worse.” A single well-explained failure is more useful to a reader than four unexplained ones, but it isn’t evidence that the strategy
behind it is the weaker choice.

I can walk through exactly what went wrong in the one confirmed case, because the citation trace is right there in the transcript, task `ew_trap_3`.

The setup: session 1 established that an “engaged customer” means a qualifying usage event in the trailing 45 days. Session 6 revised that to 30 days. Session 28 asks how many engaged customers are on the Enterprise plan, under the current (post-revision) definition. The correct answer is 22. The agent answered 28 — the exact 45-day count for that segment — and cited session 1, the original decision, as its source. Not session 6. Not “no source.” Session 1, specifically, which is exactly the trap’s predefined stale source. That’s what makes it `interference_confirmed` rather than just a wrong number: the citation trace proves which memory the agent trusted.

Here’s the retrieval call that caused it. RAG’s top-4 BM25 hits for this task’s query were sessions 15, 22, 11, and 1 — three earlier consumption questions that share almost identical phrasing with this one (“using the ad hoc engaged customer’ lookback window… how many engaged customers are there [in X]?”), plus the original establishing session. Session 6 — the one session that actually contains the revision, phrased entirely differently (“the team re-reviewed the numbers and decided the… window was too loose… changing it from 45 days to 30 days”) — never made the top 4. Its content was indexed like every other session; nothing about the pipeline skipped it. It’s lexically distant from every consumption question, precisely because a revision
announcement doesn’t ask a question at all. For this query, BM25 ranked four sessions that share the question’s vocabulary above the one session that quietly changed the answer — the update announces, once, in different words, and never comes up again. (Whether this generalizes into “BM25
buries revisions” is exactly the n=1 problem I flag below — one trace shows the mechanism, not its rate.) The agent didn’t choose to trust a dead fact over a live one. It was handed four documents, three of which quietly agreed with each other on the old number, and the one that mattered wasn’t in the stack it saw.

That’s a retrieval-ranking failure, and I want to name it precisely: the correction was in the index the whole time. Nothing was missing from storage. What failed was recall at k=4 for a chunk whose content matters enormously but whose phrasing doesn’t resemble the questions asked about it afterward — the RAG equivalent of a change-log entry that never gets surfaced because nobody searches using the words a change log uses. Full-history replay doesn’t have this specific failure mode because it has no retrieval step to fail — the revision is just there, in the transcript, whether or not it’s lexically similar to the current question. Whether that makes full-history strictly “safer” in general, or just safer against this one untuned BM25 configuration at top-4, is a question this single trace can’t answer on its own — see the limitations below.

Code, every run’s raw transcripts, and the analysis scripts behind every number above:

GitHub - EnigmaDevelop/agent-memory-lab: Does agent memory help or hurt? 3 memory strategies vs. a no-memory control, measured across 360 sessions with real accuracy AND cost data.

The cost surprise

I expected memory to cost more — full-history especially, since it resends a growing transcript every session. Per-minute billing data (Anthropic’s usage export, cross-referenced against each run’s exact start/end timestamps) says the opposite, and by a wide margin. These are per-seed figures: one 30-session run of one condition, averaged across seeds.

| Condition           | Cost per 30-session run (one seed) | Relative to no-memory |
|---------------------|------------------------------------|-----------------------|
| No memory (control) | $1.15                              | —                     |
| Full history        | $0.45                              | 61% less              |
| Rolling summary     | $0.32                              | 72% less              |
| RAG                 | $0.22                              | 81% less              |

So one seed across all four conditions is about $2.1, and the three-seed study landed somewhere near $6–7 — well under the $25 I’d budgeted, with room to spare for the failed experiments I’m not itemizing here. Two caveats I’d rather state than have you find. This is averaged over seeds 1 and
2, the two I have complete minute-level billing data for (seed 0’s usage fell in an export window I hadn’t pulled); they agree within about 7% per condition. And unlike the accuracy numbers, this table is not regenerable from the repo — I never logged per-call token usage, so it’s reconstructed from billing timestamps, not computed from the runs. Treat the ordering as solid and the exact figures as approximate. (I’ll also resist a tempting claim: prompt caching was wired up and demonstrably active, but since I didn’t log cache-read vs. write vs. fresh-input tokens, I can’t tell you how much of the low cost it accounts for versus the retry effect below. Both are real; their split is unmeasured.)

The no-memory control — the condition with the smallest context per call — was the single most expensive to run, by more than double the next strategy. And here the mechanism isn’t a hypothesis; the transcripts measure it directly. I capped each session at 8 assistant turns. No-memory used a median of 8 turns and hit that ceiling on 56 of 90 sessions— with nothing to reference, it spends every dependent and trap task retrying an answer it has no way to reach, until the budget cuts it off. All three memory strategies ran at a median of 2 turns and hit the ceiling zero times: answer on the first or second try, stop. That’s the whole cost story. A run that gives up after eight failed tries costs more than one that succeeds in two accuracy and cost weren’t a trade-off here, they moved together, for one measurable reason. (`scripts/analyze.py` section 6.)

The boring part almost sank the whole measurement

None of the numbers above would mean anything if the harness weren’t trustworthy, and the bugs that threatened that weren’t the loud kind. The dangerous ones returned a plausible wrong number and sailed past 60-plus passing unit tests: the model using SQLite’s live `now()` against data dated to a synthetic “today” (silently zeroing every date-windowed query instead of erroring), and the agent calling `answer` in the same turn as a SQL query — submitting the column alias as its final value before ever seeing the result. Both took a hard code-level block to close; neither showed up until I ran the pipeline for real and read what came back.

The statistics had a bug of exactly the same species, which is why the results section labors the point about pairing. The first analysis shuffled condition labels across the pooled 90 rows and produced a fine-looking p-value that was quietly answering a different question than the one I’d asked. Silent-and-wrong is the failure mode worth fearing in an eval harness — in the data or in the analysis of it. The loud bugs are annoying; the quiet ones end up in your chart. Nine years of data-platform work is mostly this: the unglamorous 80% is where the real risk lives.

One scoping decision belongs here too. The original plan ran a local model alongside the frontier one, but two small local models (`qwen2.5:3b`, `mistral:7b`) failed the basic tool-use task — one on a genuine small-model SQL ceiling, the other reading a correct query result and then fabricating a different number on the next turn. Neither is a story about memory, so the local arm was retired and the real run moved entirely to Claude Sonnet 5. That debugging trail is its own piece — see “Up next.”

What I’d do differently

  1. Retrieve on recency-plus-topic, not topic alone. A revision event should outrank three lexically-closer consumption questions when the topic overlaps — this is a chunking/retrieval design fix, not a bigger model fix, and it’s directly testable against this same benchmark.
  2. Measure retrieval recall directly, not just outcome accuracy. One traced failure explains one event; it doesn’t establish a general rate. Before claiming “BM25 systematically buries revisions,” the next version of this benchmark should compute recall@k for the revision session specifically, across every revisable fact, not infer a pattern from n=1.
  3. Log a “did the agent re-verify against the live source” signal, not just the final answer. Right now the judge can prove which stale session got cited; it can’t yet show whether the agent had a chance to catch itself by re-querying the database instead of trusting memory text.
  4. This is one seed-family of one fixed task set. Three reshuffled orderings of the same 30 tasks is not 90 independent draws — it’s three looks at one set. Pairing the tests fixes how the evidence is counted; it does nothing about how narrow the evidence is. The error-clustering result above is the sharp version of this: six errors, one task family, and therefore a benchmark whose difficulty is concentrated in about a fifth of its own tasks. A larger and more varied task pool is the only real fix.
  5. Nothing here tests memory at scale. Full-history’s context topped out near 4,300 tokens after 30 sessions. The interference risk everyone writes about is a large-context phenomenon, and this study stops several orders of magnitude short of it. A 300-session version — or one that deliberately grows sessions until replay stops fitting — is the experiment that would actually put full-history at risk, and I haven’t run it.
  6. I logged no token-level data, which is why the cost table is reconstructed from billing timestamps rather than computed, and why I can’t decompose the cost result into cache reads vs. writes vs. fresh input. Adding usage accounting to the client is cheap; doing it after the fact means re-running the study, which is why it’s on this list instead of in the piece.
  7. I didn’t tune the RAG chunking or retrieval count at all — 60-word sliding windows, top-4, first configuration I wrote. This specific recall failure might disappear with a larger top-k or a hybrid recency signal, and I’d want to know that before calling RAG the riskier strategy in any general sense — what this benchmark actually shows is that this RAG configuration has this failure mode, not that retrieval-based memory is inherently less trustworthy than replay.

Takeaways

  1. Having memory at all mattered far more than which kind — and skipping it wasn’t even the cheap option. No-memory control: 32% accuracy, and the most expensive condition to run. All three memory strategies: 96–100% accuracy, indistinguishable from each other on this data, at 61–81% lower cost. If your agent needs to recall its own decisions, no-memory isn’t a cheaper fallback here — it loses on both axes this benchmark measured, and the transcripts show why: the memoryless agent burned its full retry budget (median 8 of 8 turns) failing to guess answers it had no way to reach.
  2. The one confirmed false memory this benchmark found was a retrieval-ranking miss, not a “trusted stale data over fresh data” failure in the sense most interference writing assumes. RAG didn’t choose the old number over the new one — it was never shown the new one, because a correction doesn’t read like the questions that get asked about it afterward. That’s a fixable, specific, unglamorous retrieval-tuning problem, which is a more useful finding than “RAG is risky.”
  3. A citation-trace judge is what turned “wrong answer” into “provably interference” — and what kept five ordinary mistakes from being miscounted as the same thing. Without it, this piece would have one fewer real number, six unexplained wrong answers instead of one traced failure and five filed-separately slips, and an unfalsifiable guess about why RAG got that trap task wrong.
  4. The measurement scaffolding was where most of the risk was, not the models. Two silent harness bugs and one wrong statistical unit would each have produced a publishable-looking number that was answering the wrong question. If you take one operational thing from this: the bugs that survive your unit tests are the ones that return a plausible value.
